title: Probability Definitions
content: Defines `probAllDistinct k d` as the finite product $\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(1 - i/d)$, which equals the probability that $k$ people all have distinct birthdays among $d$ possible days. The collision probability is its complement $1 - P(\text{all distinct})$. These generalize the classical birthday problem from $d = 365$ to arbitrary $d$, enabling applications to hash functions and other uniform random models.

title: Fundamental Inequality: 1 − x ≤ exp(−x)
content: Proves the key analytic inequality $1 - x \le e^{-x}$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ by applying Mathlib's `add_one_le_exp` (which states $1 + t \le e^t$) with $t = -x$. This inequality is tight at $x = 0$ and is the workhorse that converts each multiplicative factor of the product into an exponential, enabling the passage from a product to a sum in the exponent.

title: Factor Nonnegativity and Boundedness
content: Establishes that each factor $(1 - i/d)$ is nonneg when $i < d$ and at most 1 when $d > 0$. These auxiliary lemmas are needed for `Finset.prod_le_prod`, which requires nonneg lower bounds to propagate a pointwise inequality through a product. The proof uses `sub_nonneg` and `div_le_one` from Mathlib's ordered field API.

title: Product-to-Exponential Bound (Sum Form)
content: The central technical step: applies $1 - i/d \le e^{-i/d}$ factor-by-factor via `Finset.prod_le_prod`, then collapses the product of exponentials into a single exponential via `Real.exp_sum`. This yields $\prod_{i<k}(1 - i/d) \le \exp\!\bigl(-\sum_{i<k} i/d\bigr)$. The three-step proof structure (pointwise bound → product of exp → sum in exponent) is a clean demonstration of how multiplicative product inequalities translate into additive exponential bounds.

title: Gauss Summation Formula
content: Proves $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} i = k(k-1)/2$ by induction on $k$, then divides by $d$ to obtain the closed form $\sum_{i<k} i/d = k(k-1)/(2d)$. This is the formula attributed to young Gauss summing $1 + 2 + \cdots + 99$ and is what gives the birthday bound its characteristic quadratic dependence on $k$. The inductive proof uses `Finset.sum_range_succ` and `ring` for the algebraic simplification.

title: Main Asymptotic Bound (Closed Form)
content: The headline result: combines the product-to-exponential bound with the Gauss sum to obtain $P(\text{all distinct}) \le \exp\!\bigl(-k(k-1)/(2d)\bigr)$. This closed-form bound is the rigorous version of the well-known approximation $P \approx e^{-k^2/(2d)}$ used throughout cryptography and probability theory. The proof is a direct rewrite of the sum form using `gauss_sum_div`.

title: Collision Probability Lower Bound
content: Takes the complement of the main bound to obtain $P(\text{collision}) \ge 1 - \exp\!\bigl(-k(k-1)/(2d)\bigr)$. This is the form most commonly cited in cryptographic analyses: the actual collision probability is always at least as large as the exponential approximation predicts. The proof is a one-line `linarith` from the upper bound on $P(\text{all distinct})$.

title: Trivial Base Cases
content: Verifies the boundary conditions: with 0 or 1 people, all birthdays are trivially distinct (empty/singleton products equal 1), and the collision probability is 0. These provide sanity checks and base cases for inductive reasoning about the birthday problem.
mathContext: $P(\text{all distinct with } k=0) = P(\text{all distinct with } k=1) = 1$

title: Probability Bounds: [0, 1] Containment
content: Proves that $P(\text{all distinct}) \in [0, 1]$ and $P(\text{collision}) \in [0, 1]$ for $k \le d$. The upper bound uses `Finset.prod_le_prod` with the fact that each factor is at most 1; the lower bound uses nonnegativity of all factors. These ensure the definitions behave as genuine probabilities.

title: Threshold Characterization
content: Proves that if $k(k-1)/(2d) > \ln(1/(1-p))$, then $P(\text{collision}) > p$. This characterizes the exact threshold: for the classic 50% case, setting $p = 1/2$ gives $k(k-1)/(2d) > \ln 2 \approx 0.693$, which with $d = 365$ yields $k(k-1) > 506$, explaining why $k = 23$ (since $23 \times 22 = 506$). The proof converts the logarithmic condition into an exponential bound via `Real.exp_lt_exp` and `Real.exp_log`.

title: Consistency with Parent File
content: Verifies that `probAllDistinct k 365` specializes to the exact same product formula used in the parent birthday problem file. This is proved by `rfl` (definitional equality), confirming that the generalization to arbitrary $d$ is a true extension of the original $d = 365$ formalization.

title: Monotonicity: More People → More Collisions
content: Proves that $P(\text{all distinct with } k+1) \le P(\text{all distinct with } k)$: adding one more person can only decrease the probability that all birthdays are distinct, since the product gains one more factor that is at most 1. The proof uses `Finset.prod_range_succ` to split off the last factor and `mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left` to bound it. This establishes that collision probability is monotonically increasing in the number of people.
mathContext: $P(\text{all distinct}, k+1, d) \le P(\text{all distinct}, k, d)$ for $k+1 \le d$
